name: Careful Company: File-Transfer Egress
description: Blocks outbound file transfer: scp/pscp/sftp/psftp/WinSCP to a remote \ destination, scripted FTP and `tftp put`, rsync to a remote, rclone to a \ remote, cloud-storage uploads (`aws s3 cp` local->s3://, `s3api put-object`, \ `az storage blob upload`, azcopy, `gsutil cp`->gs://, b2/s3cmd/mc/wrangler \ r2/supabase), peer-to-peer senders (croc/wormhole/ffsend/Taildrop), WebDAV \ mounts, and copy LOLBins (`esentutl /y`, `print /D:`, `diantz`). Package \ publishes and git remote-URL changes warn.

destructive_patterns.name: scp-destination-unverified
destructive_patterns.description: scp/pscp has a runtime-dependent or malformed destination whose perimeter cannot be verified.
destructive_patterns.explanation: The final transfer target is supplied through shell expansion or malformed remote syntax, \ so the engine cannot prove that it remains on this workstation or inside the organization. Use a \ literal local path or reviewed internal host before retrying.

destructive_patterns.name: scp-to-remote
destructive_patterns.description: scp with a remote destination copies local files off this machine.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
In `scp SOURCE DEST`, a `user@host:path` in the final position means the file is going \ out. The reverse order (`scp user@host:/data/f .`) is a download and is not matched, and \ copies to internal hosts are whitelisted.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Copy to an internal host (RFC1918, *.internal/*.corp, or a bare intranet name) \ - Ask the operator to perform the transfer

destructive_patterns.name: transfer-script-with-visible-put
destructive_patterns.description: An sftp/WinSCP command with a visible put uploads the named file.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
When the `put` (or WinSCP `/upload`) is on the command line, the direction is not in \ doubt: a local file is going to the remote side. `echo put secrets.zip | sftp -b - \ user@host` is the same operation with the command supplied on standard input.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Use `get` if the intent was to fetch \ - Transfer to an internal host instead

destructive_patterns.name: sftp-remote-session
destructive_patterns.description: An sftp session to an external host is an interactive transfer channel.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
An interactive `sftp` session can `put` any readable file, and nothing about which files \ appears on the command line. This warns rather than blocks because the same session is \ equally often used to fetch something.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Use an explicit one-shot copy so the transfer is visible \ - Connect to an internal host

destructive_patterns.name: opaque-transfer-script
destructive_patterns.description: A scripted sftp/ftp/WinSCP session runs transfer commands that are not visible here.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`sftp -b batch.txt host`, `ftp -n -s:cmds.txt host`, and `winscp /script=file` read \ their operations from a file, so whether this is an upload or a download cannot be \ determined from the command line. Warned rather than blocked precisely because the \ direction is unproven — the same standard applied everywhere else in this preset. A \ visible `put` on the line raises it to the blocking rule above. The stdin form \ (`sftp -b -`) is excluded from this warning so the whole pipeline remains visible to \ that higher-confidence rule.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Print the batch/script file first so the operations are reviewable \ - Transfer to an internal host instead

destructive_patterns.name: rsync-to-remote
destructive_patterns.description: rsync with a remote destination copies local files off this machine.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
As with scp, the remote endpoint in the final position means data is leaving. \ `rsync src user@host:/dst`, `rsync src rsync://host/mod`, and `rsync src host::mod` are \ all the outbound direction.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Sync to an internal host \ - Reverse the operands if the intent was to pull data in

destructive_patterns.name: tftp-put
destructive_patterns.description: tftp put uploads a local file to a remote host.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`tftp -i host put C:\data.bin` uploads over an unauthenticated, unencrypted protocol. \ `get` is the download direction and is not matched.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Use an authenticated internal transfer path

destructive_patterns.name: rclone-to-remote
destructive_patterns.description: rclone copying to a configured remote sends data to that provider.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`rclone copy C:\repo remote:path` uploads to whatever cloud provider `remote:` is \ configured for. A remote name needs at least two characters, so a Windows drive letter \ (`D:`) is never mistaken for one and purely local copies are unaffected.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - `rclone copy remote:path C:\local` (the download direction) is not matched \ - `rclone lsd` / `rclone about` to inspect a remote without moving data

destructive_patterns.name: rclone-stream-or-publish
destructive_patterns.description: rclone rcat/link/serve streams data out, mints a public URL, or exposes a local directory.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`rclone rcat remote:file` writes standard input straight to a remote with no local path \ on the command line; `rclone link` mints a shareable public URL for an object; \ `rclone serve http|webdav|ftp` publishes a local directory as a network service.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Use an internal share for anything that needs to be reachable \ - `rclone ls`/`lsd` to inspect without exposing

destructive_patterns.name: aws-s3-upload
destructive_patterns.description: aws s3 cp/sync/mv from a local path to s3:// uploads data to S3.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
The operand order decides the direction: a local source followed by an `s3://` \ destination is an upload. The reverse (`aws s3 cp s3://bucket/key .`) is a download and \ is not matched.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Reverse the operands if the intent was to fetch \ - Use an internal artifact store for outbound copies

destructive_patterns.name: aws-s3-api-upload
destructive_patterns.description: s3api put-object uploads a local file to S3.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`aws s3api put-object --body C:\data.zip` uploads without the `s3 cp` shape, so a rule \ keyed on operand order would miss it. (`create-multipart-upload` only reserves an \ upload id and moves no bytes, so it is deliberately not matched.)

\ Safer alternatives: \ - `aws s3api get-object` / `list-objects` for the read direction \ - Use an internal artifact store for outbound copies

destructive_patterns.name: aws-s3-presign
destructive_patterns.description: aws s3 presign mints a URL that anyone holding it can fetch.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`aws s3 presign s3://bucket/key --expires-in 604800` transfers nothing itself, but it \ produces a link that grants unauthenticated access to the object for up to a week — \ egress by reference. It warns rather than blocks because sharing a time-limited link is \ also a legitimate way to hand a large file to a reviewed recipient.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Grant access through IAM rather than a bearer URL \ - Shorten `--expires-in` and confirm who will receive the link

destructive_patterns.name: azure-blob-upload
destructive_patterns.description: az storage blob upload / azcopy sends local files to Azure Storage.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`az storage blob upload -f C:\data.zip` and `azcopy copy "C:\repo" \ "https://acct.blob.core.windows.net/c?<SAS>"` upload to a storage account, frequently \ authenticated by a SAS token embedded in the URL rather than by a managed identity.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - `az storage blob download` for the read direction \ - Confirm the storage account belongs to the organization

destructive_patterns.name: gcs-upload
destructive_patterns.description: gsutil/gcloud storage cp from a local path to gs:// uploads data to Cloud Storage.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
As with S3, the operand order decides direction; a local source with a `gs://` \ destination is an upload.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Reverse the operands to fetch instead \ - Use an internal artifact store

destructive_patterns.name: object-store-cli-upload
destructive_patterns.description: b2/s3cmd/mc/wrangler r2/supabase upload local files to object storage.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`b2 upload-file`, `s3cmd put`, and `wrangler r2 object put` are upload verbs by name. \ `mc cp`, `s3cmd sync`, and `supabase storage cp` take a direction, so those require a \ local source with a remote alias destination — the reverse order is a download and is \ not matched.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Use the corresponding download/list verb to inspect \ - Confirm the bucket belongs to the organization

destructive_patterns.name: peer-to-peer-file-send
destructive_patterns.description: croc/magic-wormhole/ffsend/Taildrop send files directly to another party.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
These tools exist to hand a file to someone else across the internet, usually via a \ relay and a short code. There is no read-only mode and no organizational control point \ in the path.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Use the company's file-sharing system so the transfer is logged

destructive_patterns.name: webdav-remote-mount
destructive_patterns.description: Mounting a WebDAV/HTTP location as a drive creates a file-copy channel over the web.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`New-PSDrive -Root \\host@SSL\DavWWWRoot\path` and `net use Z: http://host/dav` mount \ an internet location as a drive letter. Once mounted, an ordinary `copy` moves data out \ with nothing suspicious on the command line — the `@SSL` and `DavWWWRoot` markers are \ the only tell.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Map internal SMB shares (`\\fileserver\share`), which this pack does not match \ - Use the approved file-transfer path

destructive_patterns.name: copy-lolbin-to-remote
destructive_patterns.description: esentutl /y, diantz, and print /D: copy files to a remote share while posing as other tools.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`esentutl /y source /d \\host\share\out` copies files that are *locked* by another \ process — live databases, credential stores — which an ordinary copy cannot touch. \ `diantz` writes a cab straight to a UNC path and `print /D:\\host\share` copies a file \ while claiming to print it. None of these is a normal way to move data.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Use `Copy-Item`/`robocopy` for legitimate copies (this pack does not match those) \ - Stop the process holding the file rather than copying it while locked

destructive_patterns.name: package-publish-to-registry
destructive_patterns.description: Publishing a package uploads the project's contents to a registry.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`npm publish`, `cargo publish`, `twine upload`, `nuget push`, and friends upload the \ built package — which for many projects includes the source — to a registry that is \ usually public and, once published, effectively permanent. Warned rather than blocked \ because releasing is legitimate work; publishing to a local path or an internal registry \ is whitelisted.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - `npm publish --dry-run` / `cargo publish --dry-run` to check without uploading \ - Publish to the internal registry (`--registry`/`--source` pointing at an internal host)

destructive_patterns.name: git-remote-url-change
destructive_patterns.description: Adding or repointing a git remote changes where a later push sends the repository.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`git remote set-url origin <url>` is subtler than adding a remote: every subsequent \ `git push` looks completely routine while going somewhere new. `git config \ remote.origin.url` does the same without the `git remote` wording. Warned rather than \ blocked because repointing a remote is also ordinary maintenance.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - `git remote -v` to see the current remotes before changing them \ - Confirm the new host is organization-controlled

destructive_patterns.name: git-push-explicit-url
destructive_patterns.description: Pushing to a URL instead of a named remote sends the repository to an ad-hoc destination.
destructive_patterns.explanation:
`git push https://host/repo.git HEAD:main` needs no configured remote at all, so the \ destination never appears in `git remote -v` and leaves no trace in the repository \ config. Credentials embedded in the URL are a further signal. Ordinary \ `git push origin main` is not matched.

\ Safer alternatives: \ - Push to a configured remote by name \ - Confirm the URL's host is organization-controlled
